title: Why does Circular Reference cause Indirect Leak?
body_html:
From other questions on stackoverflow, I know that circular reference could cause leak, particularly indirect leaks:

Memory leak using shared_ptr Possible Memory-leaks with smart pointers

I want to follow up the issue in more details. I made the following program to illustrate the scenario:

#include <iostream>
#include <memory>
using namespace std; 

class MyClass {
public:
    MyClass()                                         { cout<<"Default constructor"<<endl; }
    MyClass(MyClass const& s)                         { cout<<"Copy constructor"<<endl; }
    MyClass(MyClass&& s) noexcept                     { cout<<"Move constructor"<<endl; }
    auto operator= (MyClass const& s)     -> MyClass& { cout<<"Copy Assignment"<<endl; return *this; }
    auto operator= (MyClass&& s) noexcept -> MyClass& { cout<<"Move assignment"<<endl; return *this; }
    ~MyClass()                                        { cout<<"Destructor"<<endl; }
    shared_ptr<MyClass> next;
};

void funct(shared_ptr<MyClass> & cl1){
    shared_ptr<MyClass> cl2 = make_shared<MyClass>();
    cout<<"**init cl2**"<<endl;
    cout<<"address cl2 points to: "<<cl2.get()<<endl;
    cout<<"count reference of cl2: "<<cl2.use_count()<<endl;
    cout<<"**link cl2 <-> cl1**"<<endl;
    cl2->next = cl1;
    cl1->next = cl2;
    cout<<"address cl1 points to:  "<<cl1.get()<<endl;
    cout<<"count reference of cl1: "<<cl1.use_count()<<endl;
    cout<<"address cl2 points to:  "<<cl2.get()<<endl;
    cout<<"count reference of cl2: "<<cl2.use_count()<<endl;
    // cl2 is deleted after exit of this function
}

int main()
{
    cout<<"Size of MyClass "<<sizeof(MyClass)<<endl;

    cout<<"**init cl2**"<<endl;
    shared_ptr<MyClass> cl1 = make_shared<MyClass>();

    funct(cl1);

    cout<<"**cl2 is destroy**"<<endl;
    cout<<"count reference of cl1: "<<cl1.use_count()<<endl;
    cout<<"count reference of cl1->next "<<cl1->next.use_count()<<endl;
    cout<<"address cl1->next points to "<<cl1->next<<endl;   // print the object's address where cl2 points at.  
    return 0;
}

SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: 64 byte(s) leaked in 2 allocation(s).

Other answer explain that the leak occurs because "they [the object] have pointers to each other which keeps them alive." I don't understand that well - meaning I don't understand the C++ mechanism or rules that "pointer keeps them alive". I output the ownership count of each object here.

Question 1: Why do cl1 still have ownership of 2 when cl2 is already gone after funct returns? In other words, who have the ownership of the object the cl1 points to beside cl1 pointer?

Question 2: someone commented that when I have cl1->next = cl2, a copy of the smart-pointer object is created. When the life-time of the variable cl2 ends, the copy still lives, and points to the very same memory. Would someone be able to prove that?

I edited my program to have both copy and assignment constructor. I see that nothing is printed out beside the default constructor.

If both the cl2 pointer itself and the memory where it points to is deallocated, then who else is cl1->next? Anyhow, I don't see any destructor is called. The address where cl2 points to at still lives, as printed out in main, near the end of the program.

cout<<"address cl1->next points to "<<cl1->next<<endl;   // print the object's address where cl2 points at.

What I have tried:

  • I tried to create circular reference between 2 objects.
  • I print out ownership to check if the ownership changes and could go to zero when the program exists.
  • I check the indirect leak size expect that each leak should be same as the object size. But each leak is twice the object size. Total leak is 4 times the object size.

events.body_html: With cl1->next = cl2 you create a copy of the smart-pointer object. When the life-time of the variable cl2 ends, the copy still lives, and points to the very same memory. If you check cl1->next.use_count() when back in the main function, you should notice that it's 1.

"Why do cl1 still have ownership of 2 when cl2 is already gone" -- Why does this look like a problem to you? If two people (let's call them "Clark1" and "Claire2") own a company (let's call the company "Two"), and one of them retires, would you expect that to force the other person to retire?
Please don't ask multiple questions, it's a bad fit for a site where you can only accept one answer. And, hint: examine the value of cl1->next after the function returns.

@Someprogrammerdude I have edited the question a bit to clarify and address the main issue I want to ask. What still have ownership of the object where cl2 originally point to.   I made copy and assignment constructor to see if there is any copy of the MyClass object, but there is none printed out.   Why isn't destructor of cl2 is called?

That's kind of the point of a shared ownership structure like std::shared_ptr. You can have multiple owners to a single resource, and if one owner releases its ownership (like when cl2 is destructed) the resource still lives on because there are other owners.

Perhaps it might be easier to visualize if you draw it using pen and paper? Draw three labeled boxes on a paper, label one cl2, one cl1->next and the last one MyClass object. Draw an arrow from cl2 to MyClass object, and also draw an arrow from cl1->next to MyClass object. That's kind of how the ownership and sharing of the MyClass object is. When later cl2 is destructed, you can erase that box and its arrow from the drawing (or redraw without cl2), you see that the object still exists and with a live pointer to it.
